name: Hoeryong Revolutionary History Museum
funding: State museum in Hoeryong, two storeys, centred on the activities of Kim Jong Suk.
watch: Photos are allowed inside, unlike many such museums, Koryo Tours says. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
why_flagged: State museum in Hoeryong, two storeys, centred on the activities of Kim Jong Suk.
affiliations_note: Stands a short walk from the Native House of Kim Jong Suk, a site in the same city.

overview: Two-storey white concrete museum in the centre of Hoeryong (Koryo Tours).
It centres on the revolutionary activities of Kim Jong Suk, born in Hoeryong, wife of Kim Il Sung and mother of Kim Jong Il (Koryo Tours).
Koryo Tours says the entrance hall holds a large painting of her with her infant son on a horse, and the halls show relics, tools and possessions of the guerrillas who operated around Hoeryong.
It is a short walk, over a hill, from the Native House of Kim Jong Suk and from the statue of her at the city's centre.
Korean Wikipedia's page on Hoeryong lists a Kim Jong Suk revolutionary history museum that opened in October 1974 (translation).
Koryo Tours says photos are allowed inside, unlike many other revolutionary history museums, and that guides welcome questions.
details.funding_verdict: Hoeryong Revolutionary History Museum (Hoeryong): state-run: a state museum
funding: Koryo Tours says many North Korean cities have revolutionary history museums with the same core narrative, and that Hoeryong's local story is Kim Jong Suk.

The state announces its budget only as yearly percentage changes. KCNA claimed on 24 March 2026 that 2026 revenue would reach 100.5% of 2025 and spending 105.8%, with funds for the cultural sector at 103.1% of last year's.

red_flags.heading: Sanctions, state body
points: Executive Order 13722 of 15 March 2016 blocks property of the Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party of Korea that is in the United States or in the control of US persons (Federal Register, 18 March 2016). The museum is a state body, and the order does not name it.

not_related: the Native House of Kim Jong Suk, a separate site in the same city (Koryo Tours).
details.bottom_line: The museum is a state museum paid for by the North Korean state. The Sanctions basis is the weak point: the Government of North Korea is blocked under Executive Order 13722.

name: International Friendship Exhibition
funding: Opened 1978, this state museum holds gifts to Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il from foreign dignitaries. KCNA claimed hundreds of thousands of gifts from some 160 countries (1998).
watch: Estimates of the gift count run from 60,000 to 220,000 (Wikipedia). The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
why_flagged: Opened 1978, this state museum holds gifts to Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il from foreign dignitaries. KCNA claimed hundreds of thousands of gifts from some 160 countries (1998).
records_note: It is a state institution, and North Korea reports its state budget only as yearly percentage changes (spending up 3.8 percent in 2025, per the Korea Institute for National Unification).

overview: State museum of gifts to Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il, at Mount Myohyang in Hyangsan County, about 160 kilometres north of Pyongyang (Korean Wikipedia, Reuters).
Opened in August 1978. KCNA said in June 1998 that it had just been built on an expansion basis (KCNA).
KCNA described a green tile-roofed building in the traditional style, without timber or windows, with light, temperature and humidity set automatically.

Koryo Tours says the exterior is concrete made to look like wood and the main building lies inside a mountain, in two large buildings, one for each leader's gifts, with gifts to Kim Jong Suk and Kim Jong Un also housed there.

The gift count varies by source: KCNA claimed hundreds of thousands from some 160 countries in 1998. Time (2009) gave 60,000, Reuters (2006) gave more than 220,000, and The Independent (1997) quoted a figure of 61,000.

Visiting: Koryo Tours says a visit takes about two hours, with a security check, metal items stored at the entrance and no photography inside. Wikipedia says shoes are removed and visitors are asked to bow before portraits.
details.funding_verdict: International Friendship Exhibition: state-funded: the Government of North Korea
funding: The collection is gifts from foreign leaders, friendship groups, notable individuals and companies (Koryo Tours); Reuters named a luxury car from the late leader of the Hyundai Group, a clock from CNN's founder and a living-room set from a South Korean furniture maker (2006).

North Korea announces its state budget as yearly percentage changes, not amounts. KCNA claimed on 24 March 2026 that 2026 revenue would reach 100.5 percent of 2025 and spending 105.8 percent, with funds for the cultural sector at 103.1 percent of last year's and 15.8 percent of spending going to national defence.

red_flags.heading: Sanctions on the state
points: US Executive Order 13722 of 15 March 2016 blocks property in US jurisdiction of the Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party of Korea; section 9 defines the Government as the DPRK government and its agencies, instrumentalities and controlled entities (Federal Register, 18 March 2016).

press.overall: Three pieces from news and magazine outlets discuss the exhibition between 1997 and 2009. Two read it as a display of the leaders' standing aimed at North Koreans.

items.title: "North Korean museum shows off leaders' gifts" (2006)
points: Reports more than 220,000 items and a guide's claim of gifts from 179 countries, and says most gifts came from communist leaders and a few figures the West treated as pariahs.
Quotes a South Korean official who visited: the museum shows North Koreans how much praise the leaders received abroad.

items.title: Stephen Vines, "The Great Leader rules from beyond the grave" (1997)
points: The headline carries the state's honorific for Kim Il Sung. The piece calls the exhibition the apex of the cult around him and quotes 61,000 presents.
Argues the display of foreign goodwill contrasts with North Korea's isolation and its reliance on aid donors, and says bowing before the leader's image is not voluntary.

items.title: Tomas Van Houtryve, "Journey to North Korea, Part II: The Pack-Rat Dictatorship" (2009)
points: A photojournalist who visited in 2007 and 2008 as part of a communist-solidarity delegation describes about 60,000 gifts in an underground hall, including an ivory ashtray from Robert Mugabe and a sabre from Yasser Arafat.
Most of the piece covers surveillance and a visit to the Kumsusan mausoleum; the exhibition gets one paragraph.

details.bottom_line: The money behind the exhibition is the North Korean state's. The weak points are the sanctions basis under Executive Order 13722 and the spread in the gift count, from 60,000 in Time to more than 220,000 in Reuters.

name: Kaesong Koryo Museum
watch: Hall 3 is left off the foreign-visitor route unless a guide opens it. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
why_flagged: State-run museum in Kaesong with over 1,000 Koryo-dynasty artefacts in four halls and an open-air stone collection; 20,000 m², 12 main buildings.
affiliations_note: Occupies the Songgyungwan academy, one of 12 components of the UNESCO World Heritage property Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong, managed by the Kaesong People's Committee.

overview: Museum of Koryo-dynasty history in eastern Kaesong, open every day according to Koryo Tours. Wikipedia puts the site about 2 km northeast of central Kaesong.
It has occupied the former Songgyungwan since 1987 (Wikipedia).

The site is the former Songgyungwan (Sungyun Academy), the highest Confucian educational institution of the Koryo dynasty. Wikipedia gives its opening as 992 and its designation as the principal teaching institute as 1089, and Koryo Tours says the academy moved to Seoul in 1394 (Koryo Tours).

The buildings burned in the Imjin War in 1592 and were rebuilt from 1602. Koryo Tours dates the reconstruction to 1602 to 1610. Koryo Tours counts 12 main and six auxiliary buildings on 20,000 square metres, Wikipedia counts 20 buildings besides Taesong Temple and Myongnyun Hall. The two sources do not agree.

Over 1,000 artefacts in four halls (Koryo Tours): Hall 1 on politics, economy and society. Hall 2 on science and culture, including movable metal type and celadon. Hall 3 a 1.6 m iron Buddha from Chokjo Temple. Hall 4 on metalwork, sculpture and painting. An open-air exhibition by a stream holds stone pagodas and stupas from former Kaesong temples.
Visiting: Koryo Tours says Hall 3 is usually left out of tours for foreign visitors.
details.funding_verdict: Kaesong Koryo Museum: owner and funder not named in any page opened
funding: A Seoul Shinmun report of 12 October 1991 gave no funding or operating details and said only that the North Korean authorities generally pay some attention to preserving the city's historic sites.

In October 2015 the museum hosted a special exhibition of finds from the joint North and South Korean excavation of the Manwoldae palace site, organised by South Korea's Cultural Heritage Administration, the Ministry of Unification and the South-North Historians Council (Ajunews, 15 October 2015). That joint dig began in 2007.
details.bottom_line: The weak point is that no ownership, budget or board is published. Worth watching: any published word on ownership, and further joint excavation exhibitions such as the 2015 one.

name: Korean Art Gallery
funding: Workers' Party of Korea state budget.
watch: The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
why_flagged: National fine-art museum with 22 display rooms; KCNA claimed 6 million cumulative visitors by 2020. Budget unpublished.
records_note: The national arts portal's page on the museum, read from an archive copy, gives its history only.

overview: National art museum on the south side of Kim Il Sung Square, Pyongyang. Koryo Tours calls it the Korean Central Art Museum.
Opening year: Koryo Tours says 1954. Wikipedia and Koryo Studio say 1948 (Wikipedia gives 11 August 1948 and also tags it 1954). The sources do not agree. Koryo Studio says it was renovated in 2010.
Four storeys and 22 rooms (Koryo Studio, Wikipedia). Wikipedia adds an exhibition hall, preservation rooms and a study room, and over 10,000 square metres of floor space.

The tour runs from reproductions of Koguryo tomb paintings through Korean history to socialist realist works. Koryo Studio says paintings of leaders giving on-the-spot guidance are shown and some displayed works are copies because the originals are stored elsewhere (Koryo Studio).
Visiting: Monday to Saturday all year, closed on public holidays. Free. A shop sells artworks and souvenirs. Photography inside is not allowed (Koryo Tours, 13 April 2020).
Visitors: Wikipedia, citing the state news agency KCNA, says over 6 million people had visited by 2020.
details.funding_verdict: Korean Art Gallery: owner and funder not named in any page opened
funding: The atlas listed the funder as the Workers' Party of Korea state budget; no page opened states this.
Wikipedia's references cite the Ministry of Culture of North Korea and the National Tourism Administration, but the article does not say either owns, funds or runs the gallery.
details.bottom_line: Its owner, budget and board are unpublished. Worth watching: any published word on who runs it, and whether its own website is ever reachable.

name: Korean Revolution Museum
funding: State museum founded 1948 as the National Central Liberation Struggle Museum and renamed 1960. KCNA claimed over 27 million visitors by 2008.
watch: On Mansu Hill since April 1972. The Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party are blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
why_flagged: State museum founded 1948 as the National Central Liberation Struggle Museum and renamed 1960. KCNA claimed over 27 million visitors by 2008.
records_note: It is a state institution, and North Korea reports its state budget only as yearly percentage changes (spending up 3.8 percent in 2025, per the Korea Institute for National Unification).
affiliations_note: KCNA describes it as an education institution of the Workers' Party of Korea.

propaganda.summary: State museum founded 1 August 1948 on Mansudae Hill to exhibit Kim Il Sung's revolutionary history. In April 2022 KCNA reported a new hall presenting Kim Jong Un's first decade, including his nuclear force declaration.

overview: State history museum on Mansu Hill in central Pyongyang, next to the Mansudae Assembly Hall, with its back façade facing the Mansu Hill Grand Monument (Wikipedia).
Founded on 1 August 1948 in the Central District of Pyongyang as the National Central Liberation Struggle Museum and renamed in August 1960 (RFA).
Opened to the public in August 1955, reopened in January 1961 east of Kim Il Sung Square, and moved to Mansu Hill in April 1972 (RFA).
KCNA counted more than 90 rooms in 2008 covering the period from the 1860s to the present, while RFA's 2016 programme and Korean Wikipedia count 100.
RFA gave the museum's size as 50,000 square metres on a 240,000 square metre site (translated from the Korean).
KCNA listed two large panoramic paintings, Pochonbo Battle and Defensive Battle on Height 1,211, among the exhibits.

Wikipedia dates a renovation with a new floor to 2011 and 2012 and a major renovation completed in 2017. State media reported on 28 March 2017 that Kim Jong Un visited the renovated museum (North Korea Leadership Watch).
A new exhibition hall opened in April 2022 for the tenth anniversary of Kim Jong Un's rise to power (Korea Herald, from Yonhap).
details.funding_verdict: Korean Revolution Museum: state-funded: the Government of North Korea, with KCNA tying it to the Workers' Party
funding: KCNA described the museum in 2008 as a centre of ideological education of the Workers' Party of Korea.

North Korea announces its state budget as yearly percentage changes, not amounts. KCNA claimed on 24 March 2026 that 2026 revenue would reach 100.5 percent of 2025 and spending 105.8 percent, with funds for the cultural sector at 103.1 percent of last year's and 15.8 percent of spending going to national defence.

red_flags.heading: Sanctions on the state and the Workers' Party
points: US Executive Order 13722 of 15 March 2016 blocks property in US jurisdiction of the Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party of Korea; section 9 defines the Government as the DPRK government and its agencies, instrumentalities and controlled entities (Federal Register, 18 March 2016).
The museum is a state institution, and KCNA ties it to the Party the order names.

press.overall: Three pieces from outlets opened discuss the museum. One analyses its political purpose, two report on its renovation and a new hall.

items.title: Im Chae-uk with host Lee Hyun-ki, "Memorial museums of North and South Korea" (2016)
points: Im, introduced as a commentator on North Korean culture, argues that memorial museums exist to present a state's or regime's legitimacy to its people (my translation of the Korean title and summary).
Says much of the exhibition centres on Kim Il Sung, and sets South Korea's Independence Hall in Cheonan, opened in August 1987, beside it as the counterpart.

items.title: "N. Korea opens new exhibition hall to mark 10th anniv. of Kim's leadership" (2022)
points: Reports, from KCNA, a hall of photos and videos on Kim Jong Un's years in power, including a November 2017 letter declaring the state nuclear force complete.
News report; it does not criticise the museum.

items.title: "KJU Visits Korean Revolution Museum" (2017)
points: Summarises state media on Kim Jong Un's tour of the renovated museum, naming the Party and state officials who attended.
A summary of state claims, not criticism; the archived copy was read because the live page refused the request.

details.bottom_line: The money behind the museum is the North Korean state's. The weak point is the sanctions basis: the order blocks both the Government and the Party that KCNA ties the museum to. Worth watching: further new halls, as in 2022.

name: Mangyongdae Children's Palace
funding: State after-school palace managed by the Korean Children's Union (Koryo Tours) and paid from the state budget. Wikipedia counts over 500 teachers.
watch: Opened on 2 May 1989 before the World Festival of Youth and Students, with 120 rooms and a 2,000-seat theatre that holds regular performances.
why_flagged: State after-school palace managed by the Korean Children's Union (Koryo Tours) and paid from the state budget. Wikipedia counts over 500 teachers.
affiliations_note: Managed by the Korean Children's Union (Koryo Tours); Wikipedia names the Korean Youth Corps instead. It is the largest of the North Korean children's palaces and is separate from the Pyongyang Children's Palace.

propaganda.summary: The palace opened in 1989 under the Korean Youth Corps. Children perform regularly for tourists, singing and dancing in praise of the nation's achievements. KCNA reports the performances as pledges of loyalty to the leaders.

overview: After-school palace on Kwangbok (Liberation) Street, in the north of Mangyongdae District, Pyongyang (Koryo Tours).
Established on 2 May 1989 ahead of the 13th Festival of World Youth and Students (Koryo Tours).
A central building with two wings stands behind a sculpture and two fountains 90 and 100 metres high, and Koryo Tours says the palace was recently refurbished.
It has 120 rooms, a swimming pool, a gymnasium, a library and a 2,000-seat theatre (Koryo Tours). Wikipedia says it employs over 500 teachers, citing a 2016 Telegraph piece.
Rooms house small groups in music, dance, foreign languages, science and technology, traditional arts and sports (Koryo Tours).
Koryo Tours says performances are held every Tuesday and Thursday, that foreigners can attend, and that most of its trips include the palace.
details.funding_verdict: Mangyongdae Children's Palace: state-run: a public facility managed by the Korean Children's Union
funding: Koryo Tours says the Korean Children's Union manages the palace; Wikipedia names the Korean Youth Corps instead. Both call it a public facility.
The state announces its budget only as yearly percentage changes. KCNA claimed on 24 March 2026 that 2026 revenue would reach 100.5% of 2025 and spending 105.8%.

red_flags.heading: Sanctions, state body
points: Executive Order 13722 of 15 March 2016 blocks property of the Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party of Korea that is in the United States or in the control of US persons (Federal Register, 18 March 2016). The palace is a public facility managed by the Korean Children's Union (Koryo Tours), and the order does not name it.

not_related: the Pyongyang Children's Palace, a separate palace north of Kim Il Sung Square, founded in 1963 (Wikipedia). Koryo Tours counts the two as Pyongyang's schoolchildren's palaces.

press.overall: One news photo report discusses the palace: a 2016 gala staged there for foreign visitors.

items.title: Damir Sagolj (Reuters photographs), "North Korean Children Perform Song and Dance for Foreign Press" (2016)
points: A gala of song and dance was held at the palace on 5 May 2016 for visiting foreign journalists and tourists, ahead of the Seventh Workers' Party Congress.
NBC says many of the orchestral, choir and acrobatic performances carried political undertones.

details.bottom_line: The palace is paid for by the North Korean state. The weak points are the Sanctions basis, since the Government of North Korea is blocked under Executive Order 13722, and the 2016 gala for foreign visitors, which NBC News said carried political undertones.

name: Mansudae Art Theatre
funding: State theatre whose resident Mansudae Art Troupe runs under the Workers' Party of Korea. Used for revolutionary opera and Party assemblies (Korean Wikipedia). Paid from party and state budgets.
watch: Completed in 1976 near the Grand People's Study House. It is a venue for the Samjiyon Band.
why_flagged: State theatre whose resident Mansudae Art Troupe runs under the Workers' Party of Korea. Used for revolutionary opera and Party assemblies (Korean Wikipedia). Paid from party and state budgets.
affiliations_note: Home of the Mansudae Art Troupe, which operates under the Workers' Party of Korea (Korean Wikipedia). It stands in Mansudae, Chung District, near the Grand People's Study House.

overview: Theatre in Mansudae, Chung District, Pyongyang, near the Grand People's Study House (Korean Wikipedia; English Wikipedia).
Opened in 1976 (Korean Wikipedia; English Wikipedia).
Used for revolutionary operas, plays and assemblies that the Workers' Party of Korea hosts (Korean Wikipedia).
A venue for the Samjiyon Band (English Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: Mansudae Art Theatre: state theatre: the Government of North Korea, with the Workers' Party of Korea as host and as manager of its resident troupe
funding: Party assemblies are held here, and its resident troupe works under the party (Korean Wikipedia).

North Korea announces its state budget as yearly percentage changes, not amounts. KCNA claimed on 24 March 2026 that 2026 revenue would reach 100.5 percent of 2025 and spending 105.8 percent, with funds for the cultural sector at 103.1 percent of last year's and 15.8 percent of spending going to national defence.

red_flags.heading: Sanctions, theatre used by the Workers' Party
points: Basis: Executive Order 13722 (15 March 2016) blocks the property of the Government of North Korea and of the Workers' Party of Korea (Federal Register).
The theatre hosts party assemblies and a troupe that works under the party (Korean Wikipedia).

details.bottom_line: The state and the Workers' Party stand behind the theatre, and Executive Order 13722 blocks both. The party's use of the building for assemblies is the point to watch.

name: North Hamgyong Province E-Library
funding: Provincial library opened in 2012 and run by the North Korean state.
watch: In 2013 a guide told DW it had 301 computers. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
why_flagged: Provincial library opened in 2012 and run by the North Korean state.
affiliations_note: Provincial library of North Hamgyong Province, linked by the national intranet to other study houses and libraries, Koryo Tours says.

overview: Two-floor provincial library in the centre of Chongjin, close to the Grand Monument statues, opened in 2012 (Koryo Tours).
The ground floor holds rooms of computers loaded with science and technical manuals, language lessons and vocational courses. Upstairs are book rooms, reading areas and lecture rooms (Koryo Tours).
Koryo Tours says an old index-card catalogue lists books in English, Chinese, Japanese and Russian.
Koryo Tours says the library is connected to the national intranet, which lets students contact other educational institutes, study houses and libraries.
In June 2013 a guide told DW's reporter the library had 301 computers. DW saw Dell machines running Windows XP and Microsoft Office, with an Internet Explorer icon on the desktop.
A DW reporter was told in 2013 that the library opens every day at 10 a.m. Koryo Tours lists it as a tour stop where visitors can look through the card index and try a computer.
details.funding_verdict: North Hamgyong Province E-Library (Chongjin): state-run: a provincial library of the North Korean state
funding: DW's guide, translating the head librarian, said every person in Chongjin can use the computers.

The state announces its budget only as yearly percentage changes. KCNA claimed on 24 March 2026 that 2026 revenue would reach 100.5% of 2025 and spending 105.8%, with funds for the cultural sector at 103.1% of last year's and for science and technology at 105.3%.

red_flags.heading: Sanctions, state body
points: Executive Order 13722 of 15 March 2016 blocks property of the Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party of Korea that is in the United States or in the control of US persons (Federal Register, 18 March 2016). The library is a state body, and the order does not name it.

not_related: the North Hamgyong Provincial Revolutionary History Museum, a separate state museum on the other side of the statues (Koryo Tours).

press.overall: One news report discusses the library: a 2013 DW account of a guided visit.

items.title: Benjamin Mack, "Behind the curtain" (2013)
points: Reports a June 2013 visit: the guide's 301-computer figure, the Dell machines and the desktop Internet Explorer icon; the guide said trying the browser was not possible and moved the group on.

Quotes Amnesty International researcher Rajiv Narayan on North Korean tourism in general: the policy has financial and propaganda reasons, and visitors see only what the authorities want them to see. He does not mention the library.

wider_context: The same DW piece quotes Greg Scarlatoiu of the Committee for Human Rights in North Korea saying he has seen no sign of improving human rights, and cites Human Rights Watch's 2013 World Report, which called arbitrary arrest and the torture and ill-treatment of detainees serious and pervasive problems.
The library is a facility of the state these assessments concern.
details.bottom_line: The library is paid for by the North Korean state. The Sanctions basis is the weak point: the Government of North Korea is blocked under Executive Order 13722. Worth watching: who supplied the Dell computers DW saw there in 2013.

name: North Hamgyong Provincial Revolutionary History Museum
funding: Provincial museum on Chongjin's central square, funded and run by the North Korean state.
watch: Stands beside the Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il statues. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
why_flagged: Provincial museum on Chongjin's central square, funded and run by the North Korean state.
affiliations_note: One of the provincial revolutionary history museums; the Koryo Tours guide says every province has one.

overview: Provincial museum on the main square of Chongjin, the seat of North Hamgyong Province, immediately next to the statues of Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il (Koryo Tours).
Koryo Tours says every North Korean province has a Provincial Revolutionary History Museum, and that this one covers revolutionary activity in the north of the country.
Exhibits include a room of slogan trees, which Koryo Tours says are officially presented as trees inscribed by Kim Il Sung's guerrilla followers.
Across the statues stands the North Hamgyong Province E-Library (Koryo Tours).
Koryo Tours says all tours are guided by museum staff, who focus on the activities of the North Korean leaders, and that photos are not allowed inside.
details.funding_verdict: North Hamgyong Provincial Revolutionary History Museum (Chongjin): state-run: a provincial state museum
funding: Koryo Tours says every province has one and that museum staff guide the visits.

The state announces its budget only as yearly percentage changes. KCNA claimed on 24 March 2026 that 2026 revenue would reach 100.5% of 2025 and spending 105.8%, with funds for the cultural sector at 103.1% of last year's.

red_flags.heading: Sanctions, state body
points: Executive Order 13722 of 15 March 2016 blocks property of the Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party of Korea that is in the United States or in the control of US persons (Federal Register, 18 March 2016). The museum is a state body, and the order does not name it.

not_related: the North Hamgyong Province E-Library, a separate state library across the statues (Koryo Tours).
details.bottom_line: The museum is paid for and run by the North Korean state. The Sanctions basis is the weak point: the Government of North Korea is blocked under Executive Order 13722.

name: North Korea Peace Museum
funding: Museum in the Panmunjom building where the 1953 armistice was signed; military personnel check visitors there and a Korean People's Army guide gives the introduction.
watch: The 1976 incident axe is on display at Panmunjom, Koryo Tours says. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
why_flagged: Museum in the Panmunjom building where the 1953 armistice was signed; military personnel check visitors there and a Korean People's Army guide gives the introduction.
records_note: A state museum with no website of its own; Koryo Tours describes it.
affiliations_note: Part of the North Korean side of Panmunjom, where military personnel check visitors and a Korean People's Army guide gives the introduction, per Koryo Tours.

overview: Museum in the building constructed to house the signing of the Korean War Armistice Agreement on 27 July 1953, in the former village of Panmunjeom in Panmun district, Kaesong. About 1.2 kilometres northwest of the Joint Security Area (Wikipedia).

Koryo Tours says the museum occupies the buildings once used by North Korean and UN officials to negotiate and sign the armistice, with the original flags and agreement under glass on a table in the centre of the room.

Wikipedia says the museum houses the weapons used in the 1976 axe incident, in which US Army Captain Arthur Bonifas and Lieutenant Mark Barrett were killed. Koryo Tours says the axe is on display at Panmunjom.
Wikipedia adds that a dove symbol sits above the door.

Koryo Tours says tourists reach Panmunjom by bus from Pyongyang (a 2 to 3 hour drive) or from Kaesong. Military personnel check visitors at the car park, and a Korean People's Army guide gives a short history before the buses go on to the museum.
details.funding_verdict: North Korea Peace Museum (Panmunjom): state-run: a museum of the North Korean state, on a site where military personnel check visitors and a Korean People's Army guide gives the introduction
funding: Koryo Tours describes the museum as set up in the armistice buildings, with military personnel at the car-park checks and a Korean People's Army guide giving the introduction.

The state announces its budget only as yearly percentage changes. KCNA claimed on 24 March 2026 that 2026 revenue would reach 100.5% of 2025 and spending 105.8%, with funds for the cultural sector at 103.1% of last year's and 15.8% of spending going to national defence.

red_flags.heading: Sanctions, state body with an army guide on the visit route
points: Executive Order 13722 of 15 March 2016 blocks property of the Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party of Korea that is in the United States or in the control of US persons (Federal Register, 18 March 2016). The museum is a state body, and the order does not name it.

Koryo Tours says military personnel check visitors at the Panmunjom car park and a Korean People's Army guide introduces the site before visitors reach the museum. OFAC added the Korean People's Army to its sanctions list on 1 June 2017 (OFAC); the notice names the army, not the museum.

details.bottom_line: The museum is paid for by the North Korean state, with military personnel checking visitors and a Korean People's Army guide introducing the site. The Sanctions basis is the weak point: the Government of North Korea is blocked under Executive Order 13722, and OFAC listed the army in 2017. Worth watching: the army's role on the visit route.

sources.note: copy of a KCNA text; state media
